props.title: May

sections.content: May (2002) stands as one of horror's most haunting character studies. Lucky McKee's directorial debut crafts a devastating portrait of isolation that belongs alongside other psychological horror masterpieces like Carrie (1976) and Repulsion (1965). Angela Bettis delivers a career-defining performance as May Canady, a socially awkward woman whose childhood trauma and loneliness spiral into obsession and violence. The film's brilliant use of doll imagery and body horror elements recalls Pin (1988) while establishing its own unique identity.

sections.content: McKee's film revolutionized the "female monster" subgenre by treating May's descent with genuine empathy rather than exploitation. Like Teeth (2007) and Jennifer's Body (2009), it explores feminine rage and alienation through a horror lens. The film's practical effects and purposefully uncomfortable intimacy scenes create a visceral experience that makes May's psychological breakdown feel devastatingly real.

The film's influence can be seen in later character-driven horror like Raw (2016) and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014), where female protagonists' isolation drives them to extreme acts. May's craftsmanship elevates it beyond simple shock value, using precise cinematography and a carefully constructed color palette to enhance its psychological elements. sections.content: May helped pave the way for a new wave of complex female antagonists in horror. Films like American Mary (2012) and The Eyes of My Mother (2016) followed its lead in presenting deeply troubled protagonists whose actions are both horrifying and tragically understandable. The film's exploration of body dysmorphia and social anxiety remains particularly relevant, influencing works like Starry Eyes (2014) and Perfect Blue (1997).
